definition: Forest located on dryland in lowland, upland, or montane areas, characterized by an intact, multi-layered strata with no signs of human intervention or logging disturbance that alters the forest structure and composition. It has high canopy density (>70%), and tree height is typically greater than 25 m, though this varies with site conditions and species composition

Forest located on dryland in lowland, upland, or montane areas that has experienced human intervention, with visible disturbance patterns such as canopy gaps and skid trails. Canopy density is reduced (often 40-70%). These areas typically occur near settlements and infrastructure due to easier access.

Area planted with oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) as the sole dominant species, providing 70–100% canopy cover in mature stands. Tree height ranges from 1–3 m in young plantations to 10–20 m at peak productivity, before replanting around 25–30 years. Oil palms are arranged in regular grid or triangular patterns, and the area is managed intensively with high accessibility for post-harvest operations

Vegetated areas cultivated with annual crops other than rice, such as maize, cassava, legumes, vegetables, sugarcane, tobacco, chilies, soybeans, peanuts, and other short-lived non-tree species. Canopy cover is highly seasonal, often reaching near-full cover during the growing season but leaving the land weedy or left fallow after harvest. Crops are typically arranged in blocks or strips on dry fields and are managed by plantation companies or smallholders in plot sizes ranging from small household fields to large estates. These systems occur from lowlands to high elevations on mineral soils.

Vegetation dominated by herbaceous plants (broadleaf or needleleaf) generally under 50 cm in height, characteristic of relatively dry tropical regions. These areas typically appear as grasslands with very sparsely distributed short trees.

A vegetation formation dominated by woody shrubs, typically less than 2 m in height, occasionally interspersed with very short trees not exceeding 5 m. Vegetation cover ranges from sparse to dense and may be homogeneous or heterogeneous in species composition. These areas commonly occur in drylands and  often develop after a disturbance.
Surface areas dominated by artificial infrastructure for human activities. This includes residential areas, villages, transmigration sites, roads, ports, and industrial zones.
Areas with no vegetation, either naturally barren or intentionally cleared, with no signs of resource extraction activities.
Surface cover dominated by water, represented as rivers, lakes, reservoirs, etc.
